name: attribution-judge set 2: unattributed policy text
status: frozen before any run on this set; written after the fix was built and before it was run on this set
aim: The failing shape: a company's or a public service's own policy or product text, with no named speaker, that is false (or true), where most sources found are news reports quoting it. The Air Canada case is not in this set.
note: Each false item is a statement an AI support or service bot gave, as reported in the press; the wording is a plain restatement, not a verbatim quote unless marked. Each true item is its opposite. Do not edit an item or an expected verdict after the first run.

items.text: Cursor is designed to work with one device per subscription as a core security feature.
items.basis: Given by Cursor's AI support agent in April 2025 (reported by Ars Technica and Wired, quoted in those reports); Cursor's co-founder replied that there is no such policy and users may use Cursor on multiple machines.

items.text: A Cursor subscription is not limited to one device.
items.basis: Opposite of P01; Cursor's co-founder, April 2025, as reported.

items.text: Businesses in New York City are allowed to go cashless and refuse to accept cash.
items.basis: Told to users by New York City's MyCity business chatbot (The Markup, March 2024); New York City has required most stores and restaurants to accept cash since 2020.

items.text: New York City law requires most stores and restaurants to accept cash.
items.basis: Opposite of P03; NYC Local Law 34 of 2020.

items.text: Landlords in New York City do not have to accept tenants who pay with Section 8 housing vouchers.
items.basis: Told to users by the MyCity chatbot (The Markup, March 2024); the New York City Human Rights Law bars refusing tenants for their lawful source of income, including vouchers.

items.text: New York City law bars landlords from refusing tenants because they pay with Section 8 housing vouchers.
items.basis: Opposite of P05; NYC Human Rights Law, source-of-income protection.

items.text: In New York City it is legal for a landlord to lock a tenant out of their home.
items.basis: Told to users by the MyCity chatbot (The Markup, March 2024); lockouts are illegal in New York City.

items.text: Locking a tenant out of their home is illegal in New York City.
items.basis: Opposite of P07; NYC Administrative Code unlawful eviction provisions.

items.text: In New York City, an employer may fire a worker for complaining about sexual harassment.
items.basis: Told to users by the MyCity chatbot (The Markup, March 2024); retaliation for a harassment complaint is unlawful under city, state and federal law.

items.text: In New York City, it is illegal for an employer to fire a worker for complaining about sexual harassment.
items.basis: Opposite of P09; NYC Human Rights Law retaliation provision and Title VII.
